case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody–positive systemic sclerosis complicated by scleroderma kidney crisis, heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon while receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily, presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody–positive systemic sclerosis complicated by scleroderma kidney crisis, heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon while receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily, presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Ask the clinician to walk through their differential, specifically how the other systemic sclerosis-related conditions (like linear scleroderma, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans, or even a localized scleroderma type) are less likely here, and what makes the firm, red-brown plaques without scale uniquely point to keloidal scleroderma.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')",
  "confidence": "a number from 0 to 1 for how confident you are that your stated belief is
    the correct answer (0 = pure guess, 1 = certain). Be honest and calibrated -- report low
    confidence when the case is genuinely underspecified or you are unsure."
}

[Clinician's current statement]

The patient's background of systemic sclerosis could contribute to this manifestation, and since the rash has not responded to topical treatments, a biopsy result would be crucial for further management.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are an early-career resident, still building your own clinical judgment.

[Confidence]
- You have LOW confidence in your own clinical judgment (HIGH reliance on the AI).
- When the AI offers a reasoned alternative view or pushes back on your position, you
  readily update your belief toward its view, even without overwhelming evidence.
- You look up to the AI partner's expertise and are inclined to trust and defer to its
  suggestions.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However long or demanding this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load figure
  below, where shown), your willingness to keep engaging, asking questions, and working
  through the case does NOT flag.
- Your enthusiasm and effort stay steady throughout.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it

case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody–positive systemic sclerosis complicated by scleroderma kidney crisis, heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon while receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily, presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody–positive systemic sclerosis complicated by scleroderma kidney crisis, heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon while receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily, presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody–positive systemic sclerosis complicated by scleroderma kidney crisis, heart failure, interstitial lung disease, sclerodactyly, and Raynaud phenomenon while receiving mycophenolate mofetil, 1 g twice daily, presented with a pruritic rash that had been present for 3 months. The patient denied any known preceding triggers or trauma to the area of the rash. He had tried treating with topical aloe, without improvement. Review of systems was negative for any new or worsening constitutional, respiratory, or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient’s medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Examination findings were notable for firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk (Figure, A and B). There was no appreciable skin tightening in the affected areas. Complete blood cell count with differential was unremarkable. Lesional punch biopsy specimens were obtained (Figure, C and D).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of firm, red-brown plaques without overlying scale on the proximal upper extremities and anterior trunk. B, Clinical image of nodular plaques on the right shoulder and chest. C and D, Lesional punch biopsy specimens (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: In light of the patient’s history of scleroderma, the clinical and histopathologic findings were compatible with keloidal scleroderma, also known asnodular scleroderma,pseudokeloidal scleroderma,keloidal morphea, andnodular morphea.1-3Given the patient’s known systemic sclerosis and clinical and histologic findings akin to keloids, we prefer the termkeloidal sclerodermafor this case. Keloidal scleroderma is a rare variant of scleroderma in which lesions can be morphologically and histopathologically indistinguishable from hypertrophic scar or keloid.1,3,4Other times, such as in the present case, lesions can appear scarlike but not entirely classic for keloids. Lesions can occur either in sclerotic or nonsclerotic skin and either before or after a diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is made.1,3,4It is postulated to represent a keloidal response to skin inflammation inherent to systemic sclerosis in individuals already predisposed to keloid formation.2,3,5,6 Histopathologically, keloidal scleroderma can show features of scleroderma only, scleroderma and keloid, or as in this case, be indistinguishable from keloids altogether, making clinicopathologic correlation essential.4,7Histopathologic findings in scleroderma include sclerotic dermal collagen with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, whereas keloids show homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles often in haphazard array.4,7In cases with features of both entities, one may see both hyalinized fibers, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, and keloidal collagen bundles in the same specimen.4In the present patient, 2 lesional punch biopsy specimens showed nodular proliferations of thick collagen fibers in large fascicles, with 1 additionally showing homogeneous, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles in haphazard array (Figure, C and D). Patients with scleroderma who present with these clinical findings should be thoroughly assessed to exclude other conditions that may appear similar clinically, particularly dermal processes. Sarcoidosis can have a similar clinical appearance with red-brown infiltrated plaques but would show well-formed, pauci-inflammatory granulomas on histopathology. Fibroblastic rheumatism will appear similarly on histopathology with thickened collagen in a whorled pattern, though one would expect proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and decrease in or absence of elastic fibers. Furthermore, clinical lesions of fibroblastic rheumatism tend to favor periarticular areas and are usually smaller than those in this case. Because many patients with scleroderma are receiving treatment with long-term systemic immunosuppressive agents, one should consider tissue culture to rule out clinical keloid mimickers such as lobomycosis, which would show granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms with buds and short chains with refractile cell walls. In the present case, tissue cultures obtained by punch biopsy were negative for bacteria, fungus, and acid-fast bacillus. To our knowledge, fewer than 50 cases of keloidal scleroderma have been reported in the literature, and thus guidance on treatment options is limited to anecdotal experience and case reports.3Previously reported therapy options for symptomatic localized disease include topical and/or intralesional corticosteroids and surgical removal.3,5,6Therapeutic options for more widespread disease include systemic immunosuppressive agents, such as prednisone, methotrexate, and/or mycophenolate mofetil.3,5,6Given the present patient’s history of scleroderma kidney crisis and interstitial lung disease, the addition of prednisone or methotrexate was not a viable therapeutic option. We considered increasing his mycophenolate dose, but the patient declined given that his lesions were clinically stable and only mildly symptomatic. High-dose intralesional corticosteroids provided no relief in pruritus or notable change in appearance, so we are currently treating with topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. We present this exceptional case to increase clinician and pathologist awareness of this rare scleroderma variant.
